name: Lama (Togo)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ourso, Meterwa A. 1989. Lama phonology and morphology. PhD diss., University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (IDEALS repository blocked, 403); also Brinneman & Ulrich 1995, Une grammaire du lamba (SIL Togo).
earlier_scan.note: Lama is a Gur tone language; Ourso 1989 phonology is where any stress/prominence statement would be.

new_statements.quote: The tonal system. Lama has two basic tones, a high tone and a low tone. These tones combine to give two contour tones, a falling tone and a rising tone. The latter is never realized phonetically. It always surfaces as a low tone. [...] The falling tone is only realized phonetically on the final syllable of a word (said in isolation). In phrase medial position, the falling tone simplifies to a level high tone [...]. Lama starts then with two basic tones which in turn combine to give two additional tones. The overall tone configurations are High, Low, High-Low, and Low-High in the underlying representation. At the surface level only the first three configurations are allowed. The syllable, to which we now turn, is the tone bearing unit.
new_statements.citation: Ourso, Meterwa A. 1989. Phonological processes in the noun class system of Lama. Studies in African Linguistics 20(2): 151-178. (DOI 10.32473/sal.v20i2.107452)
new_statements.locator: p. 154, section 2.1 'Main features in Lama phonology', subsection 'The tonal system' (restated in the section summary, p. 155)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lama is a two-tone register language (H, L; contour HL surfaces only word/phrase-finally, LH never surfaces); the syllable is the tone-bearing unit, with high-tone spread one syllable rightward and downdrift. The source, like every other Lama description opened (Kenstowicz, Nikiema & Ourso 1988; Ourso & Ulrich 1990; Ulrich 1994), gives no rule for word stress and does not mention stress or accent at all; no positive claim of stress placement can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal notes: rising tone never surfaces, falling tone only at (phrase-)final position, downstep of a following H after a delinked L.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about tone on words said in isolation vs phrase-medial position (Kanté dialect). No stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Ourso's descriptions (SAL 1989 article and the 1989 dissertation) describe the Kanté (Kandé) dialect of Lama, spoken in Kéran district; Aritiba 1983/1987 and Adjinare 2006 describe the Défalé/Refal (Doufelgou) and Kpaha varieties (Ulrich 1994: 'two attested dialects: Refal (Aritiba 1987) and Kanté (Ourso 1989a)'). All are under the single Glottolog language lama1275; no dialect glottocodes are assigned.

sources.citation: Kenstowicz, Michael, Emmanuel Nikiema & Meterwa Ourso. 1988. Tonal polarity in two Gur languages. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 18(1): 77-104.
sources.note: Section 4 'Some rules of Lama tonology' (p. 91): 'Lama has three surface tones on a syllable spoken in isolation: a high..., a low..., and a fall'; claims tonology never described before; high-tone spread, low tone inert, no surface rising tones; no mention of stress (the only 'accent' is the acute-accent transcription convention for Moore).
